decisions.text: **The payments direction, and five additions to the sealed-content direction** (session 67, 2026-11-12, Fable 5.2 + Venkat; amends #101; **a design direction, not wire text**, ruled when Fable edits the RFCs and again at their close): **Venkat's principle** — payment rests on competing schemes, as identity does, so the protocol holds minimal opinion and any rail or verification scheme rides it; base cases are cards, x402 and MPP; NFT gating is not blocked and not the target. **Demand pattern:** fast, frequent, agent-driven buying under delegated spending authority is the default; people set limits and preferences; subscriptions are standing access to a class of content for a renewing period. **RFC-7 proposes no wire construct**; it is a recommendation that becomes a technical note (#90), and everything it needs is in RFC-6. **Added to RFC-6:** (1) an OPTIONAL plain-text `about` on a sealed entry, the seller's own description, never a title (#46), with one rule for readers — `about`, else the cover — and the entry's commitment proposed to bind whichever was shown; (2) the **pass**, a bare public key as a third grant recipient, for readers with no origin: static, re-fetchable, a bearer instrument; (3) a home MAY answer a request with any HTTP challenge, and the first answer to a probe is the same for everyone; (4) **epochs**: a lock keeps a stable id and each epoch has its own key, so a subscription is a standing claim on the lock and renewal is obtaining the next epoch's key; (5) **terms**: a reference to a stable document in `stub_of`'s two shapes, a pinned blyg version or a plain URL, on a wrap, optionally on a grant, and on an item or manifest for public content — a citation and never enforcement, no rights vocabulary, never a gate for readers, never a mention. This is the protocol's first rights construct of any kind. **The door:** the request URL answers 402 in the rail's own format; hold, probe, then ask; `rel="payment"` for a person; two doors per entry, the entry's and the lock's. **No price, currency, rail or for-sale flag in any protocol document** (Venkat agreed). **The assumptions are written down** (plan §8.1, thirteen, agent-first buying the first, each with what to revisit if it is wrong) and RFC-7 must carry them as its own section. **Without an origin:** pay at a storefront, redeem a voucher (opaque evidence, no wire text) into a pass; a `redeem` verb goes to RFC-4's handler. **Disclosed, not ruled:** reversal, third-party homes holding lock keys, paid content travelling with quotes, on-chain member lists. **Rent and purchase (revised the same session, Venkat's question; narrows #101's refusal):** the wire does not choose. A held key keeps working, so what a lapsed subscriber keeps is decided by which keys the home hands out — *holding* (epoch lock keys: everything in the paid epochs, read with no traffic) or *on demand* (one entry key per item opened, free under the subscription: the home stops answering on lapse, at the cost of seeing every first read). Rent is the expected default; the RFC states the trade-off and recommends neither. A lapsed grant is proposed as a **retention event** (plan §9 item 15: a conforming reader drops the key and decrypted copies, as on withdrawal; cooperation, said as such). **What #101 refuses is now worded as constructs on the wire that claim to restrict use after delivery** — expiry times, read counts, metering — not rental as a business model; locking out a non-cooperating reader stays impossible without per-reader serving (#93), re-encrypting the back catalogue, or a trusted runtime. Purchase is weaker than the word: an entry key opens one version, superseded versions stop being served unless pinned, and withdrawal reaches paid content, so a seller who means "buy" SHOULD pin what was sold and corrections should be free. An earlier draft of this decision imposed "a lapsed subscriber keeps what they paid for"; Venkat declined to impose it without an architectural reason, and there was none. Three strawmen (the door, the pass, the voucher) were put and composed, not chosen between. Opus drafts RFC-7 beside RFC-6; the two go to Fable and are meant to publish together. Plan: `docs/v0.5-plan.md` §3.1, §3.6–§3.9, §8, §9 items 18–24, §12 (a worked example).
